reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes an arbitrage bot with claims of effortless and recurring profits, including "$200 Daily" and 0.4–0.6% returns per trade. It directs viewers to sign up through the creator's referral link, offers free USDT, encourages recharging funds, and promotes commissions from recruiting other users. The creator presents the platform as "legit" and "safe" while soliciting deposits and referrals rather than merely reporting on or testing a third-party scam.

opening.argument: Judge, the speaker does not present arbitrage prices as fixed: he says they fluctuate rapidly, which makes the opportunity time-sensitive rather than certain. He also offers a way to test the application using the sign-up credit instead of adding funds. After the example, he says he *thinks* the account is in profit, a narrower claim than independently verified returns. These qualifications matter when assessing whether the video promises viewers a guaranteed outcome.

citations.quote: these prices fluctuate a lot. In a second, it fluctuates up and in a second, it fluctuates down.
if you don't want to recharge you. Can use the two dollars you'll be getting for free from me and test run this application

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening rightly points to automated trading and projected earnings, but a projection from a stated capital amount is not proof that every viewer will earn it. The recharge option is paired with a no-recharge test, and the speaker himself describes changing prices. Those details limit how confidently the pitch can be read as an unconditional profit guarantee.

citations.quote: So imagine you have a thousand dollars on this robot right now

these prices fluctuate a lot.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Acknowledging price movement is not a warning about losing deposited funds, and an optional trial does not change the solicitation. The speaker tells viewers the bot will perform the opportunity without their involvement, projects recurring earnings, and directs them to his referral link. His tentative wording about one displayed result does not qualify those broader claims.

opening.argument: Judge, the video spends substantial time demonstrating what the speaker sees inside the application. He starts with exchange-price differences, then describes initiating a single run and checking the trade record. The profit he reports is a small change in his displayed account figure, not evidence that he has independently tested large-scale returns. Read in that context, the video can be understood as an operational walkthrough of a trading tool, even though the presenter speaks favorably about it.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution cites the earnings projection and referral structure, but neither erases the demonstrated workflow. The speaker explicitly calls his purpose a practical example and shows the claimed trade records. That does not validate the app; it does mean the video contains more than an unsupported instruction to deposit money.

citations.quote: i'm only here to come and show you a practical example of how to earn with this. Arbitrage bought
so here are the records of the trades we made and here are also the records of where we. Bought and sold

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A walkthrough can itself be the vehicle for promotion. Here the demonstration is tied to claims of automated profit, a monthly earnings projection, and an invitation to use the speaker's referral link. Records displayed within the promoted application do not independently establish that exchange trades occurred or that viewers can realize those returns.

citations.quote: By itself without you doing anything
you are now making. 120 dollars plus every month
if you sign up with my own referral link
here are also the records of where we. Bought and sold

opening.argument: Judge, the sign-up incentive and referral commissions are openly described, not hidden. The speaker says the viewer may test with the credited two dollars without recharging, and describes commissions as additional to, rather than deducted from, the referred person's money. A referral offer is not, by itself, proof that the trading service cannot work. The video does not show whether a viewer deposits, withdraws, or actually receives any projected return; those outcomes cannot be inferred from the pitch alone.

citations.quote: Sign up and Claim Your 2USDT Now:
if you don't want to recharge you. Can use the two dollars you'll be getting for free from me and test run this application
that doesn't mean it is going to be removed from. Your own money no i'm going to get it for free

rebuttal.rebuttal: The referral tiers deserve scrutiny, but the cited percentages describe what the speaker says the app pays for introductions; they do not establish where that money comes from. Likewise, the presence of a recharge button establishes a funding route, not an observed deposit or failed withdrawal. The evidence supports concern about the offer, but it does not prove those unobserved outcomes.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The concern is the offer being promoted, not a claim that a particular viewer has already lost money. The speaker encourages use of a bot with the viewer's capital, projects recurring returns, supplies a sign-up link, and describes payments across multiple referral levels. The absence of an observed failed withdrawal does not turn that combined solicitation into an ordinary loyalty promotion.
